Author: simi150500
Content:
Summary from my thesis:
"The most commonly used ADCs are so-called Nyquist ADCs, which operate at a fixed sampling frequency and thus output equidistant samples [4,5]. However, certain signal groups exhibit significant variations only within short time intervals. This is particularly relevant in bio-signal acquisition and processing, where sparse signals are observed in electrocardiograms (ECGs) and electroencephalograms (EEGs). According to the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem, the sampling rate of a Nyquist ADC is determined by the highest frequency component during these transient changes [6]. This results in an unnecessarily excessive number of samples in minimal signal variation time intervals, leading to higher power consumption in data processing and transmission [7].
However, optimizing data handling and energy consumption is crucial for batterypowered, wireless, and wearable devices, such as fitness trackers, medical sensors, and Internet of Things (IoT) devices [8]. Event-based ADCs offer a promising solution by generating data points only when the signal exceeds a predefined voltage threshold [9–11]. The reduced data samples are strongly tied to savings in energy consumption, storage resources and computational effort [12]. In [13, Fig. 13], it is demonstrated that event-based ADCs consume a lot less power than the Nyquist ADC-based counterpart. As demonstrated in this work, adaptively adjusting these voltage thresholds further enhances efficiency [14]."

Author: simi150500
Content: However, the huge "problem" of this ADC is now that the data samples are non-equidistant. So things like FFTs are not possible, and therefore showing the frequency domain of the reconstructed signal is not directly possible without interpolation. Meaning, metrics like ENOB and SNDR are, strictly speaking, not really possible. This is also the topic of my paper above.

Author: namibj
Content:
I mean, you're kind of doing a dual-sided SAR that "compresses" no-change/no-trip time quanta away....
You have the lack of input sample and hold from a discrete time delta sigma, and the comparator second input fed from a DAC of a SAR.
By having two comparators, one for lower and one for upper bound, you can drive the system such that you can keep high responsivity to transients that blow outside the band between upper and lower threshold, without tripping the digital machinery and DACs and whatever resolving/positive-feedback cascade the comparator needs, if the signal stays within the band that you keep as narrow as you _want_ it to be per the requests put onto your digital control logic that decides what DAC values to feed which comparator at what time.
